data.title: Choose the correct answer for each question.
data.description: Practise combining Past Simple, Past Continuous and Past Perfect to organise events and background in narratives.
learningPoints: Use Past Simple for the main sequence of completed events.
Use Past Continuous for background actions and scenes in progress.
Use Past Perfect for events completed before another past point.
Shift tense according to foreground, background and prior events.
Avoid overusing the Past Perfect once the time sequence is clear.
Use narrative tenses to make stories coherent and easy to follow.

sections.explain: Use Past Continuous for background and Past Simple for the interrupting event.

words.word: I was driving home when I saw the accident.
I drove home when I was seeing the accident.
I had driven home when I was seeing the accident.

sections.explain: Use Past Perfect for an action completed before the main past event.

words.word: When we arrived, the guests had already left.
When we had arrived, the guests already left.
When we arrived, the guests have already left.

sections.summary: Using Past Simple for the main sequence.
sections.explain: Once the order of main events is clear, Past Simple is normally used for successive actions.

words.word: She opened the door, walked in and turned on the light.
She had opened the door, had walked in and had turned on the light.
She was opening the door, walked in and had turned on the light.

sections.summary: Using Past Continuous for scene setting.
sections.explain: Past Continuous describes an action already in progress in the background.

words.word: People were chatting while the band was playing.
People chatted while the band had played, as two background actions in progress.
People had been chat while the band was playing.

sections.summary: Explaining a past state with an earlier cause.
sections.explain: Past Perfect can explain why a past situation existed.

words.word: He was exhausted because he hadn't slept well.
He had been exhausted because he didn't sleep well afterwards.
He was exhausted because he hasn't slept well.

sections.summary: Using 'by the time' with Past Perfect.
sections.explain: An event completed before another past point often takes Past Perfect.

words.word: By the time the police arrived, the thief had disappeared.
By the time the police had arrived, the thief disappeared first.
By the time the police arrived, the thief has disappeared.

sections.summary: Returning to Past Simple after establishing earlier time.
sections.explain: After the earlier sequence is clear, Past Simple can resume for subsequent events.

words.word: He had packed his bag the night before. In the morning, he left at six.
He had packed his bag the night before. In the morning, he had left at six.
He packed his bag after he left in the morning.

sections.summary: Using a continuous background interrupted by a short event.
sections.explain: Use Past Continuous for the longer background action and Past Simple for the shorter event.

words.word: We were having dinner when the lights went out.
We had dinner when the lights were going out.
We had been dinner when the lights went out.

sections.summary: Using Past Perfect to avoid ambiguity.
sections.explain: Use Past Perfect when you need to make clear which of two past events happened first.

words.word: I realised that I had left my phone at home.
I realised that I left my phone at home after the realisation.
I had realised that I left my phone at home afterwards.

sections.explain: A narrative may use Past Continuous for background, Past Simple for the main event and Past Perfect for an earlier event.

words.word: It was raining when I reached the station, but the train had already left.
It rained when I had reached the station, but the train already leaves.
It had rained when I was reaching the station, but the train left before already.
